status: The two tomato cage photographs await John’s review.
artwork_only: Reconstructed two matching views in the real garden bed. Removed the log pile, fleece, extra cage, lattice and cane supports from the frame. Reused the real cage mesh, garden soil, plant habit and camera direction as guides. The drawn join and pegs illustrate the existing book instructions.

generator.generation:
Create one 1536×1024 landscape photorealistic instructional diptych. Two equal 768×1024 upright photographs, meeting exactly at the centre at x=768, edge to edge, zero gutter or typography. For page 167 of The Vegetable Guru. Photograph the same single real homemade tomato cage and the same part of John's Cornish home garden twice from the identical locked camera position and framing. First view shows it being joined, second view shows the completed cage supporting an outdoor tomato. Documentary photography texture, natural soil and daylight. This is a tidy view of a working garden.

REFERENCE 1, AUGUST, is the real home-garden seed. The right-hand fruiting plant and its cylindrical sheep-fencing cage are our main subject. The hedge, quiet shade and soil direction are native to that view. See the actual thin weathered dull grey wire, slightly uneven coarse rectangular grid, and log-and-hedge position. Reference 2 shows the lower rim sitting on soil and how the front of the bed reads. REFERENCE 3, MAY, shows John handling his own empty cage and is the authority for thin stiff grey sheep fencing, rough shaping and real hand scale. REFERENCE 4 has the existing book drawings for steps ONLY: sheet seam, tying two edges and pegging the lower rim in the finished picture. Do not copy the diagrams' bold tube thickness, smoothing, colour, stipple or white background.

CLEAN UP THE REAL AUGUST SPACE in both frames. Remove the entire log pile, plywood, shed/lattice/pallet clutter, foreground fleece, adjacent cage, other wire and netting, cane diagonals, vertical sticks and horizontal poles. The original soft medium-dark green hedge is now the quiet background across most of the frame, with no invented architecture. Restrained true Cornish greenery, perhaps a short unobtrusive strip of plain existing bed edging at the lower edge, rest is naturally dark garden soil with leaf crumbs and subtle plants at the furthest edge. Avoid busy competing twigs, supports, furniture, loose implements or structures. No central cane or brace in the illustrated cage, which in this book is shown standing on its own with pegs. This must remain a photographic site, not a seamless studio backdrop.

FRAME BOTH photos to the same camera from slightly above, enough to see the front and back of the open top and the cylindrical body. Both open upper hoops and the full lower rims at ground level are inside the two pictures, with at least 8% head and foot margins and around 14% side margins for the later page crops. Cylinder at the SAME distance/size, broad enough to read on a 30×38 mm book image. At each height the front wires must curve smoothly around to the back in correct perspective. Start with one single rectangular sheet of stiff sheep fencing hand-curved round, roughly twice as tall as wide. Thin believable dull silvery grey wire, the real broad openings of sheep fencing, a few natural kinks, rectangular almost square gaps. No second cage, thick bars, horizontal wires standing alone disconnected, spiral, stacked rings, chicken wire, commercial cone or plant pot. Light from the upper left catches the wire against the subdued hedge so the open grid is readable, without unrealistic thickness or excessive glow. Make both halves clear and keep the wire in focus.

LEFT, empty cage being made. Two close-fitting visibly used garden-gloved hands and short sections of sleeves enter naturally from the sides. One hand steadies the two VERTICAL cut edges that are coming together at the front-right seam of a single rectangular mesh sheet gently curved to a cylinder. In the other hand a real battered pair of red-brown handled pliers grips the short free ends of one small piece of binding wire at this seam. Exactly there we can see that short tie looping around and catching BOTH vertical cut edge wires, drawing them together; a single earlier twist is visible below. The other horizontal mesh rows are continuous around the circumference and line up on either side of their seam. Show a small straight seam gap where not yet attached. Open empty centre, complete wire cage down to natural soil. Hands stay off the top and bottom rims, no face needed.

RIGHT, finished planted cage. Same cage top, base, height, number of wires and perspective, with its now-closed vertical front-right seam and small restrained twisted wire fastenings clearly following the same line. Two modest inverted U-shaped steel ground pegs actually catch the bottom wire, one towards each side at the front, legs driven into the soil. Give them the size and installed contact of real landscape staples. The centre is rooted with ONE individual outdoor tomato from the August reference with some healthy green leaves, a few fruit trusses of varied sizes and ripeness, including one red or orange fruit lower down and some green fruit. Stems and leaf branches weave naturally through a few large holes and visibly rest on the cage in places. Space the leaves so they do not fill or hide the whole open cylinder; enough gap to see front and back wires behind the foliage. Do not draw a vertical straight stick inside or attach floating ties to the stem. Avoid an idealised showroom plant. Both photos look like actual visits to the same garden bed. No labels, framing or collage effects other than the simple centre seam.

checks.visual_review: The open rims, wire grid, pliers and ground pegs are visible in the working spread. Small binding twists read best in the full-size master. The two print crops retain the full subject.
